pedagogy.summary: Systematic listing enumerates all combinations of two categories (e.g. 3 starters × 4 mains) so that none is missed and none repeated, by working in a fixed order: hold the first choice constant, run through every second choice, then move on. Organising the combinations into a table or tree makes completeness checkable, and reveals that the total equals the PRODUCT of the number of options in each category (3 × 4 = 12) — an early foundation of multiplicative counting.
bestPractices: Model a fixed order — hold starter 1 and pair it with every main in turn, then starter 2, and so on — rather than listing haphazardly
Record in a two-way grid or tree so gaps and repeats are visible and completeness can be argued
Ask 'how do you know you've found them all?' and value the answer 'I worked systematically'
Draw out that the total = rows × columns = the product of the options (3 × 4), not the sum (3 + 4)
Start from sorting/ordering the child's random attempts to expose what is missing, then move to generating in order
Offer the tree diagram as an alternative systematic structure to the grid
keyRepresentations: Two-way grid / table (one category on the rows, the other on the columns)
Tree diagram (a branch per first choice, a sub-branch per second choice)
An ordered list generated by holding one choice fixed
The multiplication statement 3 × 4 = 12 read off the grid

learn.summary: Learners enumerate every combination of two categories (e.g. 3 starters × 4 mains) systematically — holding the first choice fixed and running through every second choice before moving on — so that none is missed or repeated. Recording the combinations in a two-way grid or tree makes completeness arguable and reveals that the total equals the PRODUCT of the options in each category (3 × 4 = 12), not their sum (3 + 4 = 7). This is an early foundation of multiplicative counting for Year 6.

activities.title: Pair and light the grid: building every meal in order
feedback: If the predicted total was 7, point out: each of the 3 starters makes 4 meals, so 4 + 4 + 4 = 3 × 4 = 12; the count is the grid's area (rows × columns = 3 × 4), whereas 3 + 4 just adds the two side counts and does not count the meals.

If the list is unordered with gaps or repeats, prompt: 'How do you know you've found them all?' and guide to the answer 'I worked systematically' — hold one category fixed and run through the other fully before changing it.

If only the diagonal (S1M1, S2M2, S3M3) was produced, note that both choices changed at once; show that a full ROW must be filled — fix starter 1 and vary the main across all four before moving to starter 2.
When the grid is complete and ordered, affirm that completeness can now be argued from the system itself, and that the whole row-by-row fill makes 3 × 4 = 12 visible as the grid's area.
activities.rationale: Starting from the learner's own random attempts and then sorting them exposes what is missing, motivating the move to systematic generation; a two-way grid makes completeness checkable and surfaces the product structure directly. A 'predict first' step confronts the add-versus-multiply error before building.
sourceClaims: Children first find all possibilities in a random way and cannot see which cases are missing; sorting their attempts exposes the gaps and teaches them to generate systematically, because having a system ensures no options are left out ('how do you know you've found them all?' — 'I worked systematically').
learnerActions: Start with 3 starters and 4 mains and first PREDICT how many different meals you think are possible before listing any — write down your prediction and say whether you think it is 3 + 4 or 3 × 4.

Begin by pairing starters and mains in any order you like, recording each meal you make in a two-way grid (starters down the side as rows, mains across the top as columns) by marking the matching cell.
Look at the grid: check whether random pairing has left scattered marked cells with empty gaps, or whether you tried to mark any meal twice. Ask yourself: have I found them all? Can I be sure?
Now switch to a fixed order: hold starter 1 and pair it with every main in turn (filling a whole ROW), then starter 2's row, then starter 3's row, until every cell is marked with no gaps.
Count the completed grid as rows × columns = 3 × 4 = 12, and compare this with your earlier prediction.
Explain how you know you have found every meal, and why the total is 3 × 4 rather than 3 + 4.
activities.intendedInsight: Working in a fixed order — fix one choice, run through every option of the other — guarantees no combination is missed or repeated, and the complete set fills a grid whose total is rows × columns, the product of the options.

activities.title: The tree-diagram route to the same complete set
feedback: If a starter branch is missing a sub-branch, point out that every starter must be paired with every main, so each branch sprouts all 4 mains.
If the child counts branches by adding (3 + 4), reconnect to the grid: 3 starters each with 4 mains is 3 × 4 = 12 end-points.
activities.rationale: Offering the tree as an alternative systematic structure to the grid gives a second representation of the same completeness-and-product idea; when every starter branch is given a sub-branch for every main, the tree ensures no options are left out. Whether it transfers better than the grid is not established, so both are offered as equivalent structures.
sourceClaims: Children first find all possibilities in a random way and cannot see which cases are missing; sorting their attempts exposes the gaps and teaches them to generate systematically, because having a system ensures no options are left out ('how do you know you've found them all?' — 'I worked systematically').
learnerActions: Draw a tree: one branch for each starter, then from each starter branch draw a sub-branch for every main.
Read each complete path from left to right as one meal (e.g. starter 1 → main 3).
Count the end-points of the tree and check it matches the grid total of 12.
Explain why each starter branch must sprout the same 4 sub-branches, so the total is 3 lots of 4 = 3 × 4.
activities.intendedInsight: A tree diagram is a second systematic structure that enumerates the same complete set; the repeated identical sub-branching is the product 3 × 4 made visible a different way.

activities.title: Check and extend: how many if a category grows?
feedback: If the total is given as 7, revisit the row-by-row fill: 3 rows of 4 is 3 × 4 = 12; the additive answer counts the individual options (starters plus mains), not the combinations.
If extending to a 4th starter yields an added rather than multiplied answer, prompt: one more starter adds one more full row of 4 mains, so 4 rows of 4 = 4 × 4 = 16.
If a missing combination is overlooked, ask which starter still needs pairing with which main — the empty grid cell names it.
activities.rationale: A short set of targeted checks (count with the common additive answer of 7 against the correct 12, a missing-combination fill, and a transfer prediction) probes product-versus-sum reasoning and completeness; such checks verify the skill but do not themselves build the systematic method, so they follow the building activities.
learnerActions: Answer 'How many meals are there altogether?' and justify whether it is 3 + 4 or 3 × 4.
Fill in a deliberately missing combination given a partly-completed grid or list.
Predict, WITHOUT listing them all, how many meals there would be if the café added a 4th starter (4 × 4 = 16), explaining your reasoning from the product structure.
Match each listed meal to its grid cell to confirm the set is complete and non-repeating.
activities.intendedInsight: The product structure lets you predict the count when a category grows without enumerating every case, confirming the skill transfers beyond the original numbers.

constraints: A completed grid or tree with reveal-on-tap can SHOW the organised set and the product, but if the learner does not build it or test completeness themselves, the systematic search and the product structure are presented rather than discovered — use it as a worked example, not as the main learning activity.

Recognition or matching checks (e.g. selecting the total, filling one missing combination) verify the skill but do not elicit the learner's own systematic enumeration method; keep an open construction task where the learner generates and orders the combinations themselves.
The structure here is inherently a flat two-dimensional grid or tree; a third spatial dimension is not needed and can obscure the rows × columns count.

A role-play dialogue may discuss the systematic method, but on its own it does not require the learner to generate and order the combinations themselves; if used, pair it with actual listing and grid-building so the learner produces the enumeration.

The additive error (3 + 4 = 7) must be confronted directly, ideally by a predict-before-building step and by reading the total as the grid's area (rows × columns), not merely noted as a possible slip.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit (arithmetic): 3 × 4 = 12 is correct and 3 + 4 = 7 is the common additive wrong answer to be avoided as the true total; 4 × 4 = 16 for the 4-starter extension is correct. No erroneous alternatives were carried into learner questions.

The 'grid's area' framing is accurate because each cell is exactly one combination, so rows × columns counts the meals; the earlier 'not the perimeter' wording was corrected because 3 + 4 = 7 is not the grid's perimeter and the contrast should be area versus the sum of the side counts.

Source citations support the general teaching principles (systematic generation; Year 6 enumeration objective) but do not establish the comparative efficacy of any specific interactive build, of the predict-first step, or of the tree versus grid; no claim of tested effectiveness is made. The DfE objective claim establishes the topic only and was not used as an activity sourceClaim where it did not support the specific teaching principle.

probeDeeper: How do you know you have listed every meal — could there be one you've missed?
How many meals are there altogether — is it 3 + 4 or 3 × 4, and why?
If the café added a 4th starter, how many meals would there be then, without listing them all?
You listed S1M1, S2M2 and S3M3. Which meals have you left out?
assess.correctAnswer: 12 meals — each of the 3 starters paired with each of the 4 mains (S1M1, S1M2, S1M3, S1M4, S2M1, …, S3M4), found by holding each starter and running through all four mains. The total is 3 × 4 = 12 (the product of the options), complete because every starter has been paired with every main.

errorPatterns.pattern: Lists haphazardly — random pairings, so meals are missed or duplicated and completeness cannot be judged
errorPatterns.nextMove: Hold one category fixed and run through the other in order; record in a grid so gaps show — 'found them all because I worked systematically'
errorPatterns.revealedBy: An unordered list with gaps or repeats; cannot answer 'have you found them all?'

errorPatterns.pattern: Predicts the total by ADDING the options — 3 + 4 = 7 — rather than multiplying, 3 × 4 = 12
errorPatterns.nextMove: Each of the 3 starters generates 4 meals, so 4 + 4 + 4 = 3 × 4 = 12; the filled grid's area is the count
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives the total as 7 and does not connect it to the rows × columns of the grid

errorPatterns.pattern: Changes both choices at once (e.g. only the diagonal S1M1, S2M2, S3M3), losing track of the remaining pairings
errorPatterns.nextMove: Fix one choice and vary the other FULLY before changing the fixed one; the grid shows the whole row must be filled
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Produces one combination per starter and stops, missing the other pairings

responseLevels.gap: Lists a few combinations at random with gaps or repeats; cannot say whether the list is complete; gives the total by adding or by guessing.
responseLevels.full: Enumerates all combinations by holding one category fixed and running through the other in order, records them so completeness is evident, justifies 'all of them' by the system, and gives the total as the product 3 × 4 = 12 explaining why — transferring to predict the count when a category grows.
responseLevels.partial: Lists many combinations and senses there is a full set, but works unsystematically (misses or repeats) or cannot justify completeness, and/or finds the total by counting one-by-one rather than as 3 × 4 — has combinations but not the systematic and multiplicative structure.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A café offers 3 different starters and 4 different mains. List every possible meal of one starter and one main, and show me how you know you have listed them all. Then tell me how many meals there are altogether, and why.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child working systematically holds one category fixed and runs through the other, produces all 12 in order, and gives the total as 3 × 4 = 12 explaining the product; a child listing haphazardly misses or repeats meals, cannot justify completeness, and often predicts the total by ADDING (3 + 4 = 7). Both the 'how do you know you've got them all?' question and the total separate systematic, multiplicative reasoning from random listing.
